briefs.argument: This is a 12-second, plot-integral use of a major-label hit — characters react to the song, making it a featured sync use. Unlicensed sync and master use exposes the production to statutory damages of up to $150,000 per work for willful infringement, and both the composition (UMPG) and the master (XO/Republic) are implicated as separate works. There is no realistic de-minimis position: courts reject de-minimis where the copyrighted work is deliberately featured and recognizable. Distribution without a license is uninsurable.

precedents.holding: Statutory damages up to $150,000 per work for willful infringement, without proof of actual harm.
precedents.relevance: Two works (composition + master) are in play; willfulness is easy to show for a knowing sync use.

precedents.holding: Recognizable, deliberately included copyrighted work in a TV scene was not de minimis and infringed.
precedents.relevance: A deliberately featured, recognizable work defeats a de-minimis defense.

briefs.argument: The use is diegetic — the song plays from a character's phone within the story world, not as underscore. But candor requires conceding: diegetic use is still a use requiring sync and master licenses; the doctrine offers no exemption for source music, and the 12-second duration with on-screen character reaction makes the work a focal element. The defense has no precedent to stand on at this prominence.

precedents.holding: Fleeting, out-of-focus, unidentifiable background use of copyrighted works was de minimis.
precedents.relevance: Cited for contrast: this use is the opposite — clear, extended, and plot-integral.

opinion.reasoning: Featured diegetic use of a recognizable hit song for 12 seconds with character interaction. Ringgold forecloses de minimis for deliberately featured works; § 504(c) exposure covers two separate copyrights. License both sync and master before any distribution, or cut/replace the cue.
